(Translation) :
In this respect too, I should like to speak more particularly to my colleagues from the province of Quebec. As I have just said in English, we have lost from 25 to 30 million dollars in revenues since 1949. I am no expert, no great constitutional lawyer, but I do think that the construction of the trans-Canada highway is a national undertaking, involving more than one province and, therefore concerns the federal authorities as such.
If my hon. friends from the province of Quebec would care to remember this, I might remind them that even Le Devoir, our autonomous newspaper in the province of Quebec, and one which does not always support the Liberal party, has been wondering for a long time why the province of Quebec was unwilling to take part in, this project.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Autonomist? It is a
nationalist newspaper.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: It has also come out for the autonomy of the provinces. Besides, Conservative members from the province of Quebec have used it on other occasions.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: That is why Mr. Duplessis does not like anyone to read it.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Anyway, in view of the magnitude of this project, which could have meant millions for the province of Quebec,
I wonder if my hon. friends who are close to the premier of Quebec could, after considering the matter, urge the premier to accept so that we might recuperate those millions of dollars which, as I said, could be used in several fields of provincial activity.
The purpose of those remarks, Mr. Chairman, is not political but I make them because, of late, we have heard complaints from rectors of some universities and from other educational leaders, and because we need all the money we can get to help those who seek secondary education, especially university students.
(Text):
Before closing I should like to remind the minister that on many occasions he has argued that the Department of Public Works should as its name implies, be the department of government responsible for public works within Canada and outside of Canada. If one looks at Hansard one finds what he said on that question in 1954, and also on July 1, 1955. I realize the minister is one of the most influential members of the cabinet, and I was wondering if he had approached his colleagues with a view to getting more public works, and also with a view to putting into effect what he had preached while he was on this side of the house.
I should like also to ask the minister if he would be kind enough to give us a statement on the removal of Ripple rock in Seymour narrows. The minister knows that this project involved one of the biggest man-made nonatomic blasts in history, and it took place on April 5 of this year. I understand that the minister was present when the rock was removed. I am sure all members of this house would be glad to hear about one of the most interesting engineering projects ever accomplished in Canada. I am certain also that the hon. Mr. Winters, who was minister of public works when this project was initiated, would read the report with a great deal of interest. I thank you, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the theme we should follow in this discussion is that the Conservatives are just the same as the Liberals, only better. A number of points have been covered by the previous speaker upon which I was intending to touch. However, I think I should remind the minister that the leisurely progress of his estimates
Supply-Public Works
so far is in keeping with the past history of the consideration of this particular department. I feel that he, in part, has engendered that atmosphere. If one looks through back issues of Hansard, one finds that the minister always took a leisurely approach to the consideration of these estimates. He was prepared to stay and stay and ask questions. I think the new members will appreciate that bit of information and they will know they are under no compulsion to finish this matter and therefore we should be here for several days considering these estimates.
When the minister was just the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra he had considerable help in creating this atmosphere from such people as the hon. member for Kamloops; the hon. member for Victoria; and the hon. member for Huron. The members of this party are always in a self-righteous position because they have never been in power and have never been debauched by any corruption that may exist in the government.
One of the points I wanted to bring up was that two years ago the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) made an interesting comment during the consideration of these estimates. He said something like this:
Last year, I made some reference to patronage. So long as you do something for my riding, I do not care how much patronage you use. So long as we get a little project, a building here and there, we shall be satisfied. The little bit of patronage that is used by the department at times does gripe a little, but, never mind, we shall stand the gripes if the minister will get busy.
This, of course, raises a nasty suspicion in my mind that perhaps patronage did exist in the Department of Public Works under this nefarious regime which ended last June. We righteous people are worried, because of the approach of the member who has been parliamentary assistant to that department, as to whether or not patronage still exists. This suspicion was increased last session when the minister, in answer to a question from a gentleman on the Liberal benches who has since moved to a more exalted realm in Quebec, suggested that the building of certain river improvements was more likely to have been placed in certain areas if the people in the area happened to be good Liberals. As I say, these suspicions are going around in our minds. We are prepared to accept that the new minister is a very forthright and very honest individual. He has made a number of public statements that no such thing as patronage is going to exist. I feel, therefore, he should be prepared now to make a statement about the patronage

Supply-Public Works
he found in the department and the steps he has taken to stamp it out. Certainly, he should say what steps he has taken to watch his erstwhile parliamentary assistant who said he did not care how much patronage there was as long as his riding got a little bit. Now that may be in keeping with the free enterprise ethics we heard stated so well yesterday. However, it seems at odds with the minister's own position, and we would like to hear more about that.
There is one more aspect of patronage I should like to mention, and this has come to the notice of those on the opposition benches. There are not many defeated Conservative candidates across Canada, and I know that makes a number of people around this chamber very happy. Those few defeated Conservative candidates that do exist have, in a few instances since the last election, come out with statements in their local papers. These statements seem to have been triggered by letters they received from the Department of Public Works or officials of that department to the effect the government, in its graciousness, is going to do something here or there. In other words, we have defeated Conservative candidates announcing government projects as a result of what seems to be a pipe line into the Department of Public Works.
Now this may just be evidence of a superior interest on the part of the defeated Conservative candidates, but it does raise suspicions. I do not believe anyone on the opposition benches ever expects, and I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra did not, to make announcements regarding works in his constituency. However, I am sure it would have bothered the hon. member if at that time the defeated Liberal candidate made the announcements. I just wondered if the minister would not consider putting an end to this whole practice. If there is going to be a post office or a latrine or anything of that kind built in the constituency, the announcement ought to be made in a dignified way by the government and the government officials concerned. As I think the minister is aware, it does raise some suspicion if a senior civil servant is in direct communication with someone who has no more official status than that of a defeated Conservative candidate. It does make the people in such a constituency believe that the only way to get something done is to apply political pressure through party channels. If that is the way it is, I think the public should know.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Are you just theorizing?

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Yes, of course, this is pure theory.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: How about an example?

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Does some hori. member want an example? I will bring him the Timmins newspaper in which there was an example about six weeks ago; the Port Arthur newspaper, and there was one about five weeks ago in the Sault Ste. Marie newspaper. I could bring all those to the hon. member's attention. These are just points which I think, because of the pure and honest approach of the minister, should be straightened out at this time.
I believe that a few moments ago I saw the hon. member for Carleton in his seat. Both he and the Leader of the Opposition have made statements about the aesthetic appearance of the public buildings that have been erected in Ottawa, and this of course applies to other parts of Canada.
I think the minister will admit that in the realm of aesthetics we are on a general topic that should be considered properly right here in his estimates. I do believe that he has an architectural branch which in its way, as has perhaps been suggested by the hon. member for Carleton, can mould the whole atmosphere of this capital city. Obviously, if we judge by the comments of the hon. member for Carleton, this-what would you call it-Liberal modern or Liberal Gothic pattern or whatever pattern is developed is not satisfactory. It is not particularly pleasing. I think at this time-and I am not being facetious-a statement on the whole architectural approach of the Department of Public Works and the people in the Department of Public Works who are responsible is in order. If we have a bunch of buildings that in slang terms are crummy in appearance, that take away from the beauty and the dignity of Ottawa as a capital city, now is the time to do something about it. I hope the minister will make a statement in that regard.
Speaking specifically about Ottawa, I also think of one of the things that has been pointed out to me a number of times as a socialist by people living in Ottawa as an example of how socialism does not work. I was told it just the other night by a lady who works in the civil service. She said, "Socialism will not work". She said, "As to these people who are government employees, unless there is some special incentive they will not do the job." "Just the other day", she said, "We were going to have a bit of new linoleum put in our office". I may say that this was a government office. She said, "It took four members of the Department of Public Works working all afternoon just to get the measurements". This is the sort of criticism that strikes to the heart of someone whose mainsprings are in socialism.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Do you not approve of that?

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
We hate to see government employees' reputations put in a bad light. I just wonder if the minister would explain what steps he has taken to keep employees, and especially the minor employees, of the Department of Public Works functioning in an efficient manner so that this kind of criticism which seems to be floating around in Ottawa will die away and the department will get the prestige and the status that I am sure it deserves.
One of the points that was mentioned and that I have encountered countless times in looking at the previous debates was this whole question of a shelf of projects. I think the .minister must answer the questions put forward by the hon. member for Levis in this connection. He made the statement -and we all remember it in the house last session- that he found no shelf of projects that we all thought was there from 1945 on. We have been given no indication by him, in that very pleasant, rambling statement of his, just what his department is doing to build up a real shelf of projects. I think that information should be forthcoming.
Another interesting point raised by the hon. member for Levis, and which I should like to stand behind, was this. It is hard to understand why, if there has been this tremendous speed-up, the estimates for the department are not much larger than they are. If there has been this 97 per cent efficiency of this particular committee, if you are projecting things into the future and if you are going ahead with the large shelf of projects, it seems to me your planning budget at the very least would have accelerated much more than it did. I therefore think we deserve a statement from the minister with regard to his planning project.
One of the other statements that I think he should give at this time, especially for new members-and I class myself as a new member and I know the hon. member for Fort William would appreciate it at the present time-is with regard to the whole relationship between the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works. They are the two departments that affect the demands of so many of our constituents. I give as an example the lakehead harbour situation. It is very hard to determine just where the impetus for development is coming from. It is hard to see just where is the jurisdiction or his connection with what seemed to be almost a casual announcement that the government is going to put $3 million or $4 million into terminal facilities at the lakehead. I might say that we should like to know this. I understand
Supply-Public Works
this will almost be a model for other harbour developments along the great lakes in connection with the seaway development.
We should very much like to know whether it is going to be a capital expenditure by the government-there is nothing in the estimates to show this-or whether it is going to be a long-term loan at a low rate of interest to the harbour commission in question. This is an extremely important matter. The people in the area are considerably enthused about the harbour commission development but I am sure there would be a good deal of hesitation if all the government was giving was merely a long-term loan and engineering advice and not a substantial capital sum to initiate it and get things under way. I therefore hope the minister will touch on that matter.
One of the other points that I should like to make-and again it was touched on by the previous speaker-was the question of the sort of equalization of expenditures and projects across the country. As you know, we have ten provinces and within those provinces we have very many places that are clamouring for projects. During the throne speech debate from almost every person who spoke we heard of a number of little things that he would like to have for his constituency that involved the Department of Public Works. Just what is the general policy of the department in trying to equate them? Is it strictly in terms of need? Is there an attempt to balance off the provinces? If there is such an attempt, I should like to know why the ratio seems to be especially heavy, in relation to population, toward Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island in these particular estimates and I should like to know why Ontario seems to come off so lightly.
One of the other points made by the previous speaker relates to the fact that the Department of Public Works are concentrating these projects in areas of high unemployment. If seasonal unemployment is going to continue to be a problem-and I think we all agree that it is going to be-the minister can be fairly sure where these areas are because from the statistics of the unemployment insurance department there are certain areas of this country, especially related to the forest industries, the pulp and paper industries, that have a winter unemployment problem. I know certain steps have been taken by the department to do something about this matter, especially in connection with repairing and painting Department of Public Works buildings. But I wonder just how close the liaison has been with the Department of Labour to determine these areas and just how policy is directed with regard

Supply-Public Works
to plans so that an area like Windsor, the lakehead or Vancouver which faces such problems consistently each year, is going to have winter projects initiated by the Department of Public Works.
I was delighted that the hon. member for Levis brought up the point about Quebec's non-participation in the trans-Canada highway arrangements because, from checking previous debates, I find that the hon. member for Three Rivers is on record as stating that this was another example of the Liberal tendency to centralize things in Ottawa. One has the feeling that perhaps a new approach is due when we have this new government. I think a very proper question to ask is whether this government is going to take steps to bring Quebec within the operation of the Trans-Canada Highway Act or whether it is going to continue to go along with nine provinces and not the ten; and if it goes along with the nine provinces and not the ten it seems to me that it is refusing to face up to the constitutional point that has been put forward by the government of Quebec. So again, since it is a long term project, I think we need to know something about it.
One of the points that I believe was dear to the heart of the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., when he was a critic in this particular field was that the trans-Canada highway was not wide enough, that the 22 foot strip led to a concentration and a wearing out of the highway so that by the time the project is completed the highway is going to be in a state of needing rebuilding. He made the point very well, I thought that a broader highway -even a 24 foot highway-would be to the best advantage. I should like to have some word on how he has gotten along in his work within the department in seeing that this is coming to pass.
One of the other things in connection with the trans-Canada highway was this. I noticed there seems to be a popular clamour from new Conservative members in Alberta and Saskatchewan to have a second trans-Canada highway instituted under the general overlordship of the federal government.
I would suggest to the minister that in certain parts of Canada we are still waiting for the trans-Canada highway itself to be completed, and that before he follows this rush of enthusiasm from the west he should begin taking steps to get the provincial governments working much faster on completing the highway as it is. I wonder whether if in this regard he would consider offering Premier Frost of Ontario some sort of bonus in order to get his department of highways working a little harder up in northwestern Ontario. We realize we are a

part of the province which tends to be neglected, and in this case we might bring federal strength to our support in order that we may be provided with facilities which the provincial government does not seem too anxious to get for us.
There was, I notice, in the press today a statement which the head of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had made to the gentlemen in the other house to the effect that his staff had been reduced but that it was carrying out its operations even more efficiently. The only point I want to make in this regard is to ask whether the minister in the light of his responsibility for this department would consider increasing the staff in those areas of the country which are not getting service now. It has been generally admitted in the house, even by the minister himself, that the small communities are not getting the housing service which the cities are receiving, and we think Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could well take on additional staff in order to do the job effectively in these small communities, and particularly in those scattered across the bush areas. We would appreciate a statement on this, especially since the corporation has proven itself to be so efficient that it can cut staff. We should like to know if the cutting of the staff is one of the reasons we are not getting better service in the hinterland. I have gathered from my investigation of the corporation's work that certain people within the organization feel they can only give better service to the small communities if they do have more staff available for this work. I know the minister will give this point sympathetic consideration.
One of the things I wish the minister would do is to tell the committee the exact difference between so-called harbour improvements and dredging. I know we could take this point up at specific places in the estimates, but while going back into this year's estimates and last year's estimates, too, it is hard for anyone trying to look at the dredging picture to see what is provided for dredging, what is provided for rock work and groins, and what comes under the general heading of harbour improvements.
In closing, I should like to say it is always a pleasure to be in the house under what I referred to earlier as the benign influence of the Minister of Public Works, and we look forward to hearing his answers to some of the points which have been made. I may tell him that I know that the other seven members of this group-and I am sure this

applies to other hon. members of this committee-are girded, and waiting with all the standard points to be brought up on specific items of the estimates. Finally, I should like to say to new Conservative members that it is traditional for even supporters of the government to stand up and make demands, so we hope to hear a long and continued chorus in this regard.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Before we move away from this first item which is, traditionally, one of general administration, and since we were talking this afternoon about the impact of federal public works on employment, I think it might be helpful if we were to consider one typical constituency for a few moments.
It is understandable that members of the opposition should be concerned about the impact of public works on employment in Canada. I think it is fair to say that the minister believes that the program of public works initiated by the government has been helpful in providing employment. But I think it might possibly be even more influential if some other members of the house were able to check out the minister's remarks in relation to some particular typical constituency. I should like for a few moments to detail the effect of the government's public works program upon my own riding which, rightly or wrongly, I feel was neglected under the previous administration.
It may be of interest to hon. members of this house in committee to have a rough idea of the extent of federal activity in the constituency which I represent, and to gauge its impact upon employment. Since the last federal election on March 31 the federal government has awarded the following contracts-I will keep the list brief so as not to detain the committee unnecessarily- first, transit shed No. 34 on pier A-l in Halifax. The contract was awarded today for $561,290. Improvements were authorized for two pavillions at Camp Hill hospital for veterans; an extension was authorized to the medical records department at the same hospital; a contract was awarded for an extension to the central heating plant, H.M.C.S. Shearwater; one of the sub-postal stations at Halifax had its roof repaired; a contract was awarded for an airport and airways surveillance site building, one of fifteen radar sites in Canada; a canteen and gear room building was authorized at the ocean terminals; and three magazines were installed in H.M.C.S. Shearwater or, at least, contracts were awarded for their construction.
A marine stores building contract for over half a million dollars was awarded in Dartmouth. This is a rather interesting one, because Liberal candidates in the last federal
Supply-Public Works
election promised that they would have this building constructed, if they were elected, on the same day as the tenders closed in Ottawa in respect of it. In addition, a contract for an air terminal building at the Halifax international airport was awarded for nearly $4.5 million. Also, the Minister of Public Works, representing the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has, since the last federal election, signed for the federal government's share of the cost of a massive new Halifax housing development representing nearly $4.2 million, and this week Canadian National Railways called the first tender towards the construction of a ten-storey $4 million addition to the Nova Scotian hotel.
These projects alone amount to more than $14 million in one constituency since March 31. When you add to these low bids, the result of tenders called since the last federal election, but for which contracts have not been awarded, for a damage control school, a canteen and office building, and a submarine battery charging building, you come to over $15 million. In addition, tenders have been called for a breakwater wharf at Carter's point; a breakwater at Ecum Secum, and for improvements at Windsor Park and Shearwater. The Minister of Public Works has authorized repairs to and an extension of the breakwater at Cooper's point. A guardhouse and gatehouse are to be constructed at H.M.C.S. Shearwater. Repairs are to be made to the C.V.D. jetty at Halifax and in his remarks this morning the minister alluded to improvements at the French cable wharf, Dartmouth, the latter involving an expenditure of $1 million. It is proposed to extend one runway at the Halifax international airport. The sum of $50,000 is required to complete the Ralston building in Halifax and it is proposed to construct an addition and make alterations to a public building in Halifax for $750,000 and one in Spryfield. These bring the total of federal government activity in construction in Halifax city and county, which surely needed it after 20 years, to just under $20 million since March 31.
I will only detain the committee a few more moments. In harbours improvement, wharves and breakwaters, these additional repairs and expenditures were authorized: repairs to skidway and plank bridge at Bear Cove; levelling up of breakwater deck to original elevation at Eastern Passage; repairs to deck and breakwater, Grand Desert; repairs to approach and deck, wharf, Herring Cove; installation of a derrick on the breakwater, John Vogler Shore, West Quoddy; gravelling and erecting barricade, breakwater, Necum Teuch; cleaning the approach and repairing cribwork at wharf, Owl's Head; repairs to

Supply-Public Works
the approach and deck of the wharf at what is probably the most beautiful natural site in Canada, Peggy's Cove; repairs to deck and stringers, wharf, East Petpeswick; erecting barricade on the wharf at Port Dufferin East; removal of debris from old wharf at Port Dufferin West; repairs to skidway at Portuguese Cove; reconstruction of part of wharf at Sambro; repairs to skidway and construction of an engine shed at Sandy Cove; repairs and improvement at the wharf at Sheet Harbour East; installation of a derrick and placing of sheathing at the wharf, Sober Island; and authority for a fourth new wharf at Factory Cove, Port Dufferin East-all of this since March 31.
I do not wish to burden the committee with a boring recitation of other projects at places the names of which might not be familiar to hon. members of the committee.

Without any fawning whatever may I say on behalf of the people of my constituency that they appreciate what this government has done to provide employment under adverse conditions.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the estimates of the Department of Public Works are assuming much more importance this year than ever on account of the serious unemployment situation in Canada and perhaps more especially due to the promises made during the last election by the Prime Minister and his followers. Despite the fact that as late as October last the Prime Minister used to say that the Liberals were grossly exaggerating the situation he and his party have finally reached the conclusion that there is a heavy quota of unemployment in Canada at the present time. I believe the figure for June indicated that approximately half a million Canadians were unemployed and this is a greater number than we have seen for a long time.
In examining the estimates before us today I was surprised at the small amount to be expended on public works projects as compared with the promises made. When he was speaking about unemployment during the election campaign the Prime Minister led us to believe that if elected his government would devote $1,185 million to inaugurating a vast public works program but an examination of the expenditures of this department as mentioned by the minister himself this morning reveals that $233 million will be spent. There is a considerable difference between these two figures.
The total appropriation for other branches of the Department of Public Works is to be $152 million and the minister said only $44,600,000 would be spent this year. There is a difference of approximately $21 million between the appropriation for last year and this year and last year the government would not consider that unemployment was a factor in our economic situation. This year everybody admits that it is a significant problem. Even those in power at the present time admit the truth of this and realize they must do something to solve the problem.
When one examines the estimates carefully one wonders exactly how many unskilled labourers will benefit through these public works projects. A great deal of mechanical apparatus will be employed in the proposed construction and this will reduce the amount of human labour involved. A close inspection of the projects also indicates that a very large proportion of it is merely the completion of work which was started under the previous Liberal government. I did not make a calculation but I was curious as to what portion of the projects represented a completion or continuation of work which had been previously undertaken.
I see that under harbours, rivers and engineering services in Newfoundland there are three projects which are to be completed

and two projects are continuations of works which had been started before. In Nova Scotia there are seven completions and four continuations. If we look at the figures we see that the larger amounts were in 195758. The others are generally smaller. In Prince Edward Island four projects are completions. In New Brunswick there is one completion and two continuations. In Quebec there are seven completions and eight continuations. In Ontario there are six completions and six continuations. These are all works which had been started or initiated by the Liberal government which was in office until June, 1957. I do not have time to look over all the projects.
In his speech this morning the minister tried to indicate that the work which is going on now, or to be done in the current year, is work initiated by the present government to try to help unemployment. When he says that I believe he is going a little too far. What we really need at this time is work which could be easily planned, work which could start right away, not work which needs a lot of engineering, a lot of preparation by the contractors themselves, but smaller projects. It occurred to me that this would have been a good time for the Minister of Public Works, now that we are in an extraordinary situation, to reinstate the practice of building protection walls, which was the custom from 1908 to 1953. Oh, I know the answer will be that it is not the responsibility of the federal government because the federal government is responsible for navigation which is responsible for the erosion of the shores of the rivers. Well, this is an opinion which has been contradicted by some of the provincial authorities who claim that under the British North America Act navigable waters are the responsibility of the federal government even if they are navigated or not. This has been contradicted by the legal officers of the department under Mr. Winters who decided that it was not their responsibility. At the time I asked the government to submit the question to a high authority. Mr. Winters, being an engineer and not a lawyer, may not have been in a position to decide the question all by himself.
If I am not mistaken we now have a lawyer at the head of the department. He is said to be a very good lawyer, at that, and I have been asking him time after time to study this question and submit it to the supreme court because, even if he is a good lawyer, even if the officers of the department are good lawyers, they are not in a position to decide in a way which will not be questioned by the provincial authorities if it is decided that it is their responsibility.
Supply-Public Works
I believe it is the responsibility of the federal government. I may be mistaken because I am not a lawyer. As I read the British North America Act I find that the federal government is responsible for navigable waters, not navigation. "Navigable" has been interpreted as meaning "navigation", and there is quite a lot of difference. The provincial authorities say they cannot believe, because a river is not navigated, the federal authorities are not responsible. I know that the Quebec government blame it on the federal authorities and the federal authorities blame it on Quebec. I believe it is time for them to go to the Supreme Court of Canada and have it decided once and for all who is the responsible authority.
Even if it is the responsibility of the provincial authorities, from 1908 to 1953 the federal government accepted the responsibility of building protection walls where they were necessary. I know that in my county the land has been eroded in one place up to 200 feet from the river. The farmer has lost this land and he wants to know who is responsible for that loss. If it is caused by nature, then we should correct it if it is at all possible and it is up to the proper authority to do it. I want to know at the present time who is responsible for it and that is what I am asking the minister.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: It is an act of God.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
That is what I am saying; if it is an act of God, and if it can be checked, there is nothing in the gospel that says we should not try to check it. I believe it can be checked and the only way it can be checked is to have protection walls constructed along the river banks. I think it is a federal responsibility on account of the British North American Act, which refers to navigable waters. It does not use the word "navigated". It says that navigable waters are the responsibility of the federal government. In many constituencies of the province of Quebec, some of which are represented by Conservative members, many of these problems can be found and we have to decide on whose door we are going to knock. I do not think the municipal governments can do it; they have not the revenues to do it. They want to know whether it is the responsibility of the federal government. If it is the responsibility of the provincial government, they want to know it. I am asking the government at this time, and especially the Minister of Public Works, to look into the question and if it is at all possible to restart the practice which was discontinued in 1953 and help the municipal authorities to settle a problem which has been a most difficult one to understand.

Supply-Public Works

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Can he tell me whether it was the policy of the last Liberal administration to construct these retaining walls on innumerable non-navigable waters in the province of Quebec?

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
As I said a while ago, under a Liberal administration from 1908 to 1911; under a Conservative administration from 1911 to 1921; under a Conservative administration from 1930 to 1935, and a Liberal administration from 1935 to 1953 it had been the custom to build part of these protection walls here and there to help the municipalities and the proprietors of those lands. I do not know whether it was legal or not. I am not a lawyer. I am not going to discuss the matter personally. I only ask the government to place it before the Supreme Court of Canada to decide where the responsibility lies. I think that is fair enough. It will not cost very much for the government to ask for a ruling. We would then be able to get a good ruling and not just the answer of the minister that they are not responsible, not just the answer of the law officers of the department that they are not responsible. When we go to the Quebec authorities the answer we get is that they are not responsible, that it is a federal responsibility. We want to know who is responsible so that we can act accordingly.
I do not think that is an unfair demand to make of the government. I do not blame anybody. This is a question of law. I do not know anything about law but I do know that the matter can be discussed and settled by the court. When we have a legal ruling we can then go to the proper authorities and ask them to act accordingly. That is what I am asking the government to do at the present time.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the minister's statement this morning and also with some amusement at what I considered a bit of embellishment at times. However, I can well understand the minister's attitude because I am quite sure he enjoys the administration of his department. You know, Mr. Chairman, we both started our younger working days in public works. We started digging ditches together. We were members of local 54 of the eternal trench diggers association. Unfortunately the minister did half as much work as I did and got twice as much pay.
However, speaking seriously, this department has grown a great deal in importance during my tenure in the house since 1945. I presume that is on account of the increasing

demand for facilities such as public buildings, harbours, and, more particularly lately, the building of the trans-Canada highway. For some years we in this group were not at all satisfied with the administration of the public works department. Some of us had rather close associations with that department in years past and from past experiences and what we observed in the house we considered that the department was bogged down in obsolete procedures, antiquated methods and there was certain evidence of a lethargy which I think was the result of a number of causes.
I think the minister will remember that we in the C.C.F. urged for years the necessity for planning, the need for surveys to indicate the possibility of future developments so they could be anticipated, the need for increased efficiency in administration, the elimination of patronage and the expenditure of the money voted by parliament yearly instead of money being voted year after year and not expended. I think a good number of our suggestions and recommendations have been listened to and put into effect. In recent years I have noticed not only from my experience in the house but from chatting with officials in British Columbia, with officials of local organizations and with the men employed by the department at various places on various jobs, that there is now, I think it is safe to say, some planning undertaken in the department. I think one evidence of that was the establishment of a properties division for the care of buildings and so forth which I think is of great importance.
There is also greater decentralization. I remember that years ago in my own constituency one pile driver crew building a wharf actually was idle for a month on full pay because the man whose tender had been accepted to deliver lumber to the wharf suddenly asked for $10 more per thousand feet. Because the legal department had to be informed and go through all its complicated procedures these men were idle for a whole month on full pay until a decision was reached authorizing the local foreman to take delivery of the lumber at the $10 increase. That was evidence of too much centralization. I think those situations have been largely overcome in recent years by considerable decentralization and the leaving of decisions of that kind to local authorities such as district engineers and with respect to lesser matters the foreman engaged on the job and so on. I think that has improved the efficiency of the department.
I also understand there has been considerable staff reorganization and some change in

the areas of regional administration so that work can be administered by certain officials of the department to better advantage having in mind geography, distance and so on. I was very glad to hear the minister say this morning that the department was undertaking surveys with respect to possible developments in the future, anticipating the future, which I think is a very wise thing indeed.
I was very pleased to hear that the department is giving consideration to standard building plans for certain types of buildings.
I could never understand why we had to suffer, in my opinion, unnecessary expense at times and quite frequently unnecessary delay drawing up a set of plans for a building that was identical as far as needs were concerned with hundreds of other buildings that were in use in Canada at the time. I am very glad that standardization of plans has been undertaken.
I want to say at this point that I think a great deal of the credit for these improvements is due to the deputy minister, the senior officials in Ottawa and throughout the country and to the loyal co-operation of a very large staff. Some have informed me personally on a number of occasions how much more they appreciate the way things are done now compared with the way they were done at times in the past. I am not criticizing the persons who had to do with these matters in the past because obsolete methods, antiquated procedures and inertia were the result of our whole attitude to public affairs and public administration. I think the improvement springs essentially from the interest of members of parliament of all parties in improving the situation and the interest of a great number of members of the staff in that direction. It is safe to say that on this account there have been considerable savings. A great deal of waste has been eliminated, a great deal of valuable time has been saved and I hope this will continue.
Before I go on to the more local aspects of my short speech this afternoon I want to deal with the question of patronage. I have been very pleased to read the minister's announcements from time to time indicating that he is taking a strong stand against patronage. I am most pleased because patronage is a virus that can undermine the efficiency of any department. I wish him every success in all he undertakes in that direction.
I have had some experience with patronage as an observer of both the Liberals and the Conservatives. On one occasion a wharf was being built in my district by a contractor. The engineer who was acting as inspector of the wharf took ill and the district engineer asked me if I would substitute for the man until he could return. I arrived on the job
Supply-Public Works
and immediately started to cull some piles that had arrived for the building of the wharf because of their diameters, sweep and so on. The next day I got a note asking me whether I knew that the piles came from a prominent Liberal. Then I began to cull some lumber because it was not up to standard and I got another note the next day asking me whether I knew that this lumber came from a sawmill owned by the Liberal member of the provincial legislature for the district.
On the third day I started to complain about the depth of the driving of the piles. They were not going down the required 15 feet. The contractor came to me and asked me whether I did not know that every inspector on his jobs always got his board and room free. Finally, some hardware arrived, some stirrup irons for bracing and that sort of thing, and they were too light according to the specifications and I complained. I got a note asking if I did not know that this hardware store was owned by a president of the Liberal association. As a result of my experience, I resigned and as promptly as possible resumed my pleasant peasant existence.
That is my experience with the Liberals, and I had a similar experience with the Conservatives. A breakwater was being built in front of the village near where I live during the Conservative administration from 1930 to 1935. I was on the committee of the local board of trade, as it was called at that time, and we were very interested in getting this work started for the very same reason we are anxious to get work started now. There was a depression, and there was unemployment. The president of the local Conservative association was all for patronage with respect to the purchase of the cedar logs for the breakwater, the hauling of the dirt, the placing of the rocks and so on. The secretary of the association was a young Englishman, from England, and he could not understand or appreciate this patronage. He objected very strongly, so the president wrote to the president of the West Kootenay Conservative association complaining of this matter. The president of the West Kootenay association wrote back and said: "I fully appreciate your concern about this matter, Tom, but we expect an election after March of next year, so in the meantime will you quietly continue scratching his back on this matter until election day, and after election day, in good Conservative fashion, tell him to go to hell."
Now, mind you, that has been my experience all through the years. There have been members of both parties who have objected to the patronage principle. Is the chairman tapping his estimates? Well, the patronage principle has been related to these estimates

Supply-Public Works
in the past, and it has been opposed by people in both parties. I am very glad to see we are getting away from that sort of thing, and that the minister is taking a stand.
After making these somewhat kind remarks, I have one complaint and that is with respect to the fact that, on occasion, I read in the newspapers that the defeated Conservative candidate has made an announcement. On several occasions I have read that the defeated Conservative candidate has been authorized to announce the commencement of certain public works, and so on. I want to say this. I quite realize that it is the government's responsibility to make these announcements, and that is very satisfactory from all points of view. I am just saying that I am sure the minister will be generous and gracious enough to see that opposition members are also notified of these proposed undertakings and announcements of developments. I am sure he could do that without dimming, in any sense whatever, the after-election glow of the defeated Progressive Conservative candidates.
I do know there is a great demand all through the country for as early a start as possible on many of these public works. I have received letters within the last two or three days from people in my constituency, good people who are seeking work and who see no opportunity of getting employment at the moment. I do urge the minister to give every consideration to starting projects that can be started without a great deal of preparation.
There is one other matter I wanted to mention and that relates to the question of airconditioning. I understand it was the policy of the former government not to instal airconditioning in public buildings. Personally I always thought that was a great mistake in view of the fact that to instal it later means a great additional expense. I had this brought home to me very forcibly when I was in Trail some short time ago. A new federal building had been erected there, and it is generally satisfactory but all the employees were regretting the fact that airconditioning had not been installed. It gets very hot in Trail in the summer months, and the staff has found it most uncomfortable to work in that building on hot days. I do urge the government to give consideration to the installation of airconditioning in federal public buildings, particularly those in larger centres and in areas where the people suffer more from the heat. I believe the extra cost is well merited by the increased efficiency and the saving in loss of time.
I want to mention one other thing with respect to administration. I suggest to the minister that when he is starting these smaller [Mr. Herridge.l
projects throughout the country he give consideration to using day labour under proper supervision wherever possible. While this may sound unusual to a number of members who possibly have not had much experience in that respect, it is possible on smaller projects, and under proper supervision, to save money by employing day labour rather than calling for tenders. Only last year we had a very nice wharf built at Nakusp by the Department of Public Works. At the time I suggested to the minister of the day that I thought it would be a good idea to use day labour if possible, and for two reasons. I was quite sure that the minister's staff was most efficient and capable of doing the work, and also it provided employment for the staff during the year. These were men who were required, during certain months of the year, for dredging purposes and things of that sort. I was quite certain there would be a considerable saving. I understand that as a result of building the wharf with day labour there has been a saving of approximately $10,000. I urge the minister to give consideration to using day labour under adequate supervision on those projects which could be undertaken to advantage in that way.
I am going to move from the general to the particular, that is I will move from the federal field into the constituency of Kootenay West. This morning I listened with interest to the list of projects in British Columbia which the minister read. I did not hear a reference to the commencement of a new building for the R.C.M.P. in Nelson. The former government purchased a site, and I understood plans were being drawn. It is a project which, if it could be started, would provide employment for quite a number of the unemployed. At the same time, I may inform the minister it is very urgently required by the R.C.M.P. in our district because we have an abnormally large staff as a result of peculiar and intentional illegalities that occur from time to time. I trust the minister will give this matter his serious attention.
I urge that adequate funds be provided for the continued dredging of the Arrow lakes, between the upper and lower Arrow lakes. There were some suggestions made in the department two or three years ago that because the paddle-wheel steamers had ceased to run there was no necessity for dredging. The tugs that are towing the logs and towing the ore down the lake actually have a deeper draft than the stern-wheelers, and for that reason the lumber people and the persons interested in transporting ore, as well as persons with other craft which are increasing on the lake throughout the years, do urge the continued provision of

adequate funds for the dredging of the narrows between the upper and lower Arrow lakes.
I come now to the question of river bank protection, which was mentioned also by the previous speaker. Certain erosion is occasioned at the turn of the river, just below Burton, and it is largely occasioned as a result of the wash from steamers or other vessels going up and down the river. I understand this erosion is recognized as a direct responsibility of the department. Some work has been done throughout the years but when I was going down the river not long ago I noticed that the mattress was getting in poor condition. I think some work on that would save the mattress that is now in place and avoid possibly a large expenditure in the future.
Also there is the question of snags. When high water occurs on the Columbia river and the Arrow lakes you find large trees or stumps floating down from the upper Columbia and they often lie in shallow water, water that is from 10 feet to 30 feet deep, and stay there. I urge that consideration be given to pulling out the snags at the end of the lower lake and at a number of other places where they have accumulated during the years. They are a great hazard to small boats, particularly at night.
I hope the work on the straightening of the Duncan river will continue. The work that has been accomplished to date has been of great value in preventing flooding of the river, thus assisting navigation proceeding from the Duncan river to Howser lake. I might say it lowered the water table about three feet on about 3,000 acres of land which the farmers in that area can cultivate much earlier in the season. The minister knows the area very well that I am speaking about.
I might also mention that there are some piles just at the end of Howser lake that were driven originally I think by the Canadian Northern when they were attempting to build along Howser lake and they have been left at the end of the lake since the early days. The drift wood from the Duncan is coming down the Duncan and into Howser lake and piling up against these piles. Local residents asked me to suggest to the minister that a few cases of dynamite would blow these piles out and prevent log-jams at that point and the consequent flooding of the surrounding territory.
I also urge the minister to give consideration to keeping the present usable wharves in repair on the Arrow, Kootenay and Trout lakes. While not as much use is made of these wharves as in the past, with the passing of the stern wheelers, we still have boat
Supply-Public Works
service between Beaton and Nakusp daily except Tuesdays in the summer months and tri-weekly in the winter months and there is a tri-weekly service between Robson and Edgewood. There are some wharves between those two points. I remember suggestions,
I think it was two years ago, that the department dismantle the East Arrow Park wharf.
I received strong representation from the local women's institute. I always find that it is a very good thing to get the women behind you if you want to get your way. Anyway the women's institute and other organizations supported my representations and the wharf was not dismantled. I think it is most fortunate. I was there only a short time ago and there were about five small boats tied up at the wharf. The wharf has a long life ahead of it. It is built of cedar logs which are in good shape. All that is required is an occasional plank and mending of that sort.
One other thing before I conclude my epistle is this. I want to bring to the minister's attention the urgent necessity for the building of a wing dam at Arrowhead where the Columbia river enters the Arrow lakes. This wing dam I remember being built originally nearly 50 years ago at very small cost. I think it cost about $3,000 or $4,000 in those days. It was a crib dam filled with rock. This was rebuilt years later but during the last war it was allowed to fall into disrepair and has not been repaired since then. As a result of that disrepair the river instead of flowing out into the Arrow lakes at its usual point, has now been diverted in towards the shore or along the fore-shore of Arrowhead and that means that instead of the silt and all that going out into the lake where it has gone previously, it goes into the steamer channel before the wharves and around the wharves and causes extra dredging on that account. Then in the winter very large ice floes drift in and surround the wharf and at times make it most difficult for the steamers to land. I have been on the boat when they have had to spend an hour or so manoeuvring around these ice floes which in some cases can be six feet and eight feet high. They are accumulations of ice that come down from the upper Columbia. A suggestion was made to rebuild this wing dam and an estimate was given at one time but I think the minister's officials misunderstood what was suggested. I think they thought the local people were suggesting a breakwater along the fore-shore of Arrowhead. But all that is required is the replacing of the old wing dam. The timber is handy and the rock is convenient. The men are idle and are available and willing to do the work.

Supply-Public Works
There is one matter I wish to mention to the minister. For some years various requests have been made for federal government assistance in the extension of the wall at Trail. Originally the portion of the wall was built at the cost of the federal government or at the expense of the federal government, I think under legislation that was passed during the last depression, as an act for works for the general advantage of Canada. Since that time numerous requests have been made for the extension of this wall and they have been rejected on constitutional grounds. I understand the government offered to pay 37J per cent of any extension carried on at the present time but that the province and the city would have to share the balance. I urge reconsideration of that offer.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I may, I should like to offer a small contribution at this stage of the committee's proceedings with regard to what is basically a question which is a burning one in Canada today. With the recession in force and difficult as it is, involving us to a considerable extent, the question asked right across the land is this: what can the government do and what should government do? What are the limits? What are the terms of reference to solve this dilemma? Certainly I hope that as a result of our experience in facing up to this general problem we shall learn valuable lessons which we can put to work in the future to solve and in many cases to anticipate, the deteriorating effect of recession.
With reference to the matter at hand and the department under discussion, there have been understandable attempts to make political capital out of situations by people who in my humble opinion should be better informed, pretending they did not know the answer that must have been clearly obvious to them. I refer to statements that have been made in this debate and which, it seems to me, have been repeated for the last six or eight months, with reference to what this government has done to give men employment.
I made some inquiries into the matter, particularly concerning this department, quite apart from public works projects concerning the number of homes built and what the investment in the building of those homes was. The figures I got indicate that it takes approximately two men one year to build a house. So in discussing the number of homes being built on a direct on-site basis the information I have been able to gather is that there are two man-years involved. The best estimate from government and other sources which I could obtain concerning the number of man-years involved in supply industries- material, prefabricated units coming to the site, and so forth-is also two man-years. A third factor, which is a little more difficult to estimate, is the fifth man in the scheme who is working in a secondary stage-such people as moving van operators.
Having acquired this information as to the number of homes built, quite apart from the activities of the former government, for which this government specifically can take the credit, it is approximately 35,000 within the last year, and multiplying this by five in terms of man-hours I think it is fair to say that this government by its specific actions has provided year-long employment in the past year for approximately 175,000 persons. As I say, there is no secret source for this

information; it is fully available to the members of the opposition and I have been surprised that they have been asking such questions.
Getting further into this field of public works activity in terms of an anti-recession factor, my personal opinion, after listening to a television address on, I believe May 20, by the President of the United States, in which he made a statement which, in my humble opinion, is not quite fair to the role of public works as an anti-recession factor, the statement is as follows:
I am determined not to get bogged down in a slow starting emergency public works program which will provide the minimum of jobs now and a maximum of budgetary headaches in the years ahead.
I believe this was quoted by one of the hon. members of the opposition as part of an argument, as I detected it, that the government should set aside public works as an anti-recession factor. If you examine that closely, it does not mean what the hon. member for Ottawa West intended or the interpretation placed on it by other members of the opposition. "Slow starting", "emergency" and "immediate number of jobs"-there are certain non sequiturs in that statement, I suggest, because of lack of sufficient planning and anticipation. This department in particular in its activities, accelerated as they were during the winter months, and I sincerely hope I have no reason to doubt that this type of effort will be continued in order to focus attention on the winter months when the unhappy by-products of unemployment hit hardest.
We are, I feel, coming out of the woods in this recession situation. There are as many guesses as to what there is ahead of us next winter as there are people, but I should like to suggest that we start now in approaching this problem of the shelf of public works on a new basis and from a new point of view. I was certainly under the impression and, I am sure, most of the people of Canada were, that this shelf of public works that used to be spoken of following the war when there was a general indication of at least a recession and at most a depression. Certain major companies in both the United States and Canada took action based on the fact that they were virtually certain that a depression or a bad recession was bound to happen, and the propaganda organized under the previous administration pretty well convinced the people of this country that they had an assurance of public works and not the type of shelf that members opposite have mentioned in terms of things like the seaway and others.
In economic terms a shelf of public works is a series of projects brought through the whole planning stage to a point where the
Supply-Public Works
gap between the shooting of a gun, the saying of "go," and the beginning of the work and the employment of people, is relatively short. It is shorter, in fact, by the period of planning that has gone before.
The arguments which have been put up to the effect that we are the beneficiaries of this shelf of public works are economic nonsense, I submit, because by no stretch of the imagination is the St. Lawrence seaway a shelf program in economic terms. I should like to suggest that the various industrial areas of this country should be arranged in terms of relative sensitiveness in terms of unemployment. As I say, we have learned a lesson from the situation last winter, and that is that when the recession first appears unemployment manifests itself most seriously in certain areas. I should like to see in future a public works program directed to projects such as housing on a truly shelf basis, and economically desirable in every section of this country. I should like to suggest that if this were done and cognizance taken of this economic sensitivity in bringing through the planning stage to the start stage and no further-I am not suggesting this will be easy; it will be difficult in many ways because of public pressure; the public is aware of these things very rapidly-the arguments will come from the constituencies and from members in many corners of the house, probably from myself at some future time, the arguments being: these are socially and economically desirable projects, why do we have to wait for a recession to achieve the benefit of these things?
I suggest this is going to require courage and planning. As I say, I am personally confident we are heading out of the woods on this situation and probably into a series of years of prosperity. There is no question of this in the minds of economists in the United States and Canada, looking at the continental economic picture. But I do urge, and I urge most strongly, that the minister and the government should not be lulled into a sense of false security, which was the reason that this government inherited a situation where we were not able to put into force these antirecession measures as quickly as we should have been able.

My understanding of that act is that it divides itself into two parts. Part 2 is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport and has to do with the removal of obstructions to navigation in a navigable river. Part 1 falls within the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works and it has to do with the construction of dams, obstacles or obstructions in a navigable water.
On orders of the day recently I asked the Minister of Public Works if an application had been made by the government of the province of Quebec for the development of power in the Lachine section and I recall that his answer was that while there had been no official approach there had been unofficial discussions. That is the way I understood the case to be. I wanted to discuss the matter because it is one which I feel should be of keen interest to all hon. members from the province of Quebec if not indeed to all hon. members of this house because the development of power in the Lachine section of the river is related to the development of power in the international section.
If I proceed further I find that if it is not now the intention of the government of the province of Quebec to develop power in the Lachine section it soon will be because the time is fast arriving when due to the development of industry on the south shore and in the area extending from Valleyfield on the west to Sorel and Varennes on the east power will be necessary.

If you will just allow me to continue, I am speaking to the point of order. The Minister of Public Works should know that part 1 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act falls under his jurisdiction and it is clearly stated in section 7 thereof that:
7. (1) The local authority, company or person proposing to construct any work in navigable waters, for which no sufficient sanction otherwise exists, may deposit the plans thereof and a description of the proposed site with the Minister of Public Works, and a duplicate of each in the office of the registrar of deeds for the district, county or province in which such work is proposed to be constructed, and may apply to the governor in council for approval thereof.
I happen to know that informal discussions have already taken place in this matter and the only place they can be conducted is through the Department of Public Works and an application to put an obstruction in a navigable river must of necessity go to the Minister of Public Works. What I propose to do now is to discuss this informal application.
I have asked for a return concerning correspondence with the government of the province of Quebec and the federal government. I have not been successful in getting it because it is not ready but there is no doubt in my mind that under part I of the Navigable Waters Protection Act this department, and only this department, is the one concerned.

The application can go to no other department. Certainly it cannot go to the Department of Transport. For that reason I feel I am in order in discussing the development of power under the estimates of the Department of Public Works and particularly under the first vote in those estimates.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think your ruling is erroneous because it puts me in the position of not being able to discuss this. However, I shall not discuss your ruling; I accept it. I should now like to go on and discuss improvements of harbour and river works along the St. Lawrence seaway. This morning the minister attempted to read out at some length some of the developments that were taking place in the various harbours from the head of the lakes to the lower St. Lawrence. My purpose in rising now is to bring to his attention the fact that the development of rivers and harbours arising out of the seaway should be an orderly one, and

I doubt very much whether it will be unless there is an economic survey made of those ports along the seaway route.
During an earlier discussion I had occasion to suggest to the government the establishment of an economic survey of the seaway and the effects it would have on the various regions of Canada. I ventured to suggest that if such a survey were established it would be possible to ascertain what effect the seaway might have on the Atlantic regions, on the regions of Ontario and Quebec, on the prairie regions and on the Pacific coast province; also I did suggest that particular attention might well be paid to the metropolitan areas of Montreal and Toronto-Hamilton because I think it would be a mistake if the government were to go about the development of harbours in the great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway area without a well conceived plan.
There is no doubt that the legislation which has already been brought down in this house, having to do with the development of the port of Hamilton and the improvements for Toronto, as well as the establishment of a harbour commission at the lakehead, are all to the good. I think, too, that consideration should be given not only to lake ports but to ports in the lower area of the St. Lawrence. It is true that the national harbours board, over which the minister has no jurisdiction, should look after the interests of harbours such as Montreal, Quebec and Three Rivers, but there are any number of other harbours in the province of Quebec which to my mind are not being given the attention they should. When I look at the amounts that are contained in these estimates for lower St. Lawrence ports I find they are only paltry; when I look at the amounts that are contained here for port developments east of the city of Montreal I find that they do not compare with items elsewhere.
It has been said in this house that upon the opening of the seaway a certain volume of traffic will by-pass the city of Montreal and that the seaway might well be detrimental to that city. I do not believe those statements. There is no doubt that a certain amount of traffic will, as it is bound to, go beyond the city but there is a large amount of new traffic, which has never come to Montreal namely the lake carriers, which will come down to Montreal for the first time and which I think will bring a volume of traffic that did not exist before.
A very recent study has been prepared by the University of Indiana, in conjunction with the Chicago board of trade, on grain movements on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence in which there are extremely interesting conclusions. One of the conclusions is

that no less than 200 million bushels of United States grain will be transported through the seaway. If that survey is accurate, then it means that this grain will come down in lake carriers, both United States and Canadian, and provision will have to be made for the development of port facilities not only at Montreal but at ports beyond Montreal for trans-shipment overseas. These ports are places such as Seven Islands, Ri-mouski, Three Rivers, Quebec, Sorel, all the ports on the lower St. Lawrence.
What provision is being made by the Department of Public Works for port facilities at Seven Islands, for instance? I see in the estimates small amounts for piers and wharves but in view of the survey on the movement of grain made by the University of Indiana in conjunction with the Chicago board of trade I think the minister should give careful consideration to whether or not additional elevator space should not be built at these ports and whether additional facilities should not be built at the port of Rimouski, for instance.

maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: In arranging this survey was there any thought given by the former government to the protection of the Canadian shipping industry having regard to the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED RESOLUTION OF FEDERATION OF MAYORS AND MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
The St. Lawrence seaway authority did not deal with the Canadian shipping industry. The authority was a crown corporation that had two things to do. One was to expropriate property from the port of Montreal to lake Erie for seaway purposes and the other was to build a canal 27 feet in depth. So far as the seaway authority is concerned, it had those two things to do. In fact, rumour has it that he might consider relinquishing the public works portfolio and devote his full time to the proceedings of this house. We hope to have him around for a long time yet.
However, the Minister of Public Works is not the only hard worker in that important department. He is ably seconded by a parliamentary assistant who is also very devoted to his job. I would not like to miss this opportunity to extend my warm congratulations to all the officials in the Department of Public Works, from the senior officials down to the lowliest employee. This department has a large and competent staff, men on whom we can rely at all times. They are sincere civil servants. Therefore, the hon. holder of that portfolio need not worry; we will try to co-operate with them.
This morning the minister attempted to demonstrate that the estimates for his department were a great deal higher at this time than they had been in the past. However, if we take a close look at these figures we will see that this year the extra amount provided is hardly 27 million dollars, even if we take into account the fact that the supplementary estimates for 1957-58 amounted to 16 or 18 million dollars, because this year, in the supplementary estimates, we find an amount of approximately 15 million dollars.
